claim: Disintegration is the reversal of transposon DNA integration at a target site and is regarded as an abortive off-pathway reaction.
source: 'Disintegration'—the reversal of transposon DNA integration at a target site—is regarded as an abortive off-pathway reaction.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background context for the study.

claim: Protospacer insertion is mechanistically analogous to DNA transposition.
source: Here, we challenge this view with a biochemical investigation of the mechanism of protospacer insertion, which is mechanistically analogous to DNA transposition, by the Streptococcus pyogenes Cas1-Cas2 complex.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract as a premise of the study.

claim: In supercoiled target sites, the predominant outcome is the disintegration of one-ended insertions that fail to complete the second integration event.
source: In supercoiled target sites, the predominant outcome is the disintegration of one-ended insertions that fail to complete the second integration event.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: In linear target sites, one-ended insertions far outnumber complete protospacer insertions.
source: In linear target sites, one-ended insertions far outnumber complete protospacer insertions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: The second insertion event is most often accompanied by the disintegration of the first, mediated either by the 3′-hydroxyl exposed during integration or by water.
source: The second insertion event is most often accompanied by the disintegration of the first, mediated either by the 3′-hydroxyl exposed during integration or by water.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: One-ended integration intermediates may mature into complete spacer insertions via DNA repair pathways that are also involved in transposon mobility.
source: One-ended integration intermediates may mature into complete spacer insertions via DNA repair pathways that are also involved in transposon mobility.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the experimental findings and mechanistic reasoning.

claim: Disintegration-promoted integration is functionally important in the adaptive phase of CRISPR-mediated bacterial immunity.
source: We propose that disintegration-promoted integration is functionally important in the adaptive phase of CRISPR-mediated bacterial immunity, and perhaps in other analogous transposition reactions.
evidence: This is the main proposal of the paper based on the experimental findings.

claim: CRISPR-based bacterial immunity uses information from a prior infection stored in the chromosome to target and destroy invading viruses or plasmids.
source: CRISPR-based bacterial immunity uses information from a prior infection stored in the chromosome to target and destroy invading viruses or plasmids.
evidence: This is background information stated in the introduction.

claim: The adaptive phase of CRISPR defense involves the deposition of short pieces of DNA (protospacers) from foreign nucleic acids into the chromosome as spacers.
source: The adaptive phase of this defense system involves the deposition of short pieces of DNA (protospacers) from foreign nucleic acids into the chromosome as spacers—the storage units of immunological memory (Hille et al., 2018; Marraffini, 2015).
evidence: This is background information stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: The CRISPR locus has a (leader-[repeat-spacer]n-repeat) organization.
source: The CRISPR locus has a (leader-[repeat-spacer]n-repeat) organization, and the long primary transcript derived from it is processed by Cas (CRISPR-associated) and/or host nucleases into mature CRISPR-RNAs (crRNAs) (Barrangou and Marraffini, 2014; Barrangou, 2015; Wiedenheft et al., 2012; Wright et al., 2016).
evidence: This is background information stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: CRISPR-Cas systems are classified into two broad categories: Class 1 systems employ a multi-protein-RNA interference complex (Cascade), and Class 2 systems utilize RNA-guided target recognition and cleavage by a single protein (Cas9 or Cas12).
source: CRISPR-Cas systems are classified into two broad categories (Brouns et al., 2008; Gasiunas et al., 2012). Class 1 systems employ a multi-protein-RNA interference complex for target recognition, termed Cascade. Class 2 systems utilize RNA-guided target recognition and cleavage by a single protein, that is, Cas9 or Cas12.
evidence: This is background information stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Self-targeting is avoided via multiple mechanisms, including recognition of a protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) immediately bordering the crRNA-complementary DNA sequence.
source: Self-targeting is avoided via multiple mechanisms, including recognition of a protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) immediately bordering the crRNA-complementary DNA sequence (Gasiunas et al., 2012; Jiang and Doudna, 2017; Jinek et al., 2012; Elmore et al., 2016; Pyenson and Marraffini, 2017; Smargon et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is background information stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: The conserved Cas1 and Cas2 proteins are essential (and sufficient in some systems) to carry out spacer acquisition in vivo.
source: The conserved Cas1 and Cas2 proteins are essential (and sufficient in some systems) to carry out spacer acquisition in vivo (Nuñez et al., 2015a; Yosef et al., 2012).
evidence: This is background information stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: In the Escherichia coli (Type I-E) and Enterococcus faecalis (Type II-A) Cas1-Cas2 crystal structures, a pair of Cas1 dimers flank a central Cas2 dimer on either side in a butterfly arrangement.
source: In the Escherichia coli (Type I-E) and Enterococcus faecalis (Type II-A) Cas1-Cas2 crystal structures, a pair of Cas1 dimers flank a central Cas2 dimer on either side in a butterfly arrangement, providing a ridge that can accommodate the pre-spacer DNA (that includes the PAM sequence), or the protospacer DNA (that lacks a complete PAM), with splayed out single strand termini (Nuñez et al., 2015b; Wang et al., 2015; Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is background information stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Protospacer integration is mechanistically analogous to DNA transposition, with terminal 3′-hydroxyls attacking the target phosphodiester bonds at the leader-repeat (L-R) junction on one strand and the repeat-spacer (R-S) junction on the other.
source: Protospacer integration is mechanistically analogous to DNA transposition, with terminal 3′-hydroxyls attacking the target phosphodiester bonds at the leader-repeat (L-R) junction on one strand and the repeat-spacer (R-S) junction on the other (Nuñez et al., 2015a; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: These transesterification reactions are carried out by the Cas1 active sites of the Cas1-Cas2 complex.
source: These transesterification reactions are carried out by the Cas1 active sites of the Cas1-Cas2 complex.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Repair of the intermediate containing the (protospacer)-(repeat) strand fusions completes the reaction with a duplication of the repeat sequence, one copy each on either side of the spacer insert.
source: Repair of the intermediate containing the (protospacer)-(repeat) strand fusions completes the reaction with a duplication of the repeat sequence, one copy each on either side of the spacer insert (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The prominent outcome of Cas1-Cas2 reaction with supercoiled plasmid was the conversion of the supercoiled plasmid into a relaxed distribution.
source: The prominent outcome was the conversion of the supercoiled plasmid into a relaxed distribution (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: The formation of a spacer integrant was barely detectable in supercoiled plasmid reactions.
source: The formation of a spacer integrant joined to the leader-proximal repeat end (L-R) on one strand and the spacer-proximal repeat end on the other (R-S) was barely detectable.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the supercoiled plasmid reactions.

claim: Supercoil relaxation by Cas1-Cas2 required the CRISPR locus to be present in the target plasmid, and was dependent on the protospacer.
source: Supercoil relaxation by Cas1-Cas2 required the CRISPR locus to be present in the target plasmid, and was dependent on the protospacer (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Optimal reaction occurred at 4:1 and 2:1 molar ratios of Cas1:Cas2, with increasing Cas2 inhibiting the reaction mildly.
source: Optimal reaction occurred at 4:1 and 2:1 molar ratios of Cas1:Cas2, with increasing Cas2 inhibiting the reaction mildly (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 1C.

claim: The predominance of the relaxed (closed circular) plasmid over the 'nicked' plasmid in the product indicates that the Cas1-Cas2 complex fails to complete protospacer integration in most cases.
source: The predominance of the relaxed (closed circular) plasmid over the 'nicked' plasmid in the product indicates that the Cas1-Cas2 complex fails to complete protospacer integration in most cases.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data from supercoiled plasmid reactions.

claim: The major in vitro activity of Cas1-Cas2 is the Sisyphean reversal of semi-integration events (disintegration) mediated by the 3′-hydroxyl exposed next to the integration junction.
source: The major in vitro activity of Cas1-Cas2 is the Sisyphean reversal of semi-integration events (disintegration) mediated by the 3′-hydroxyl exposed next to the integration junction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on supercoiled plasmid reactions.

claim: DNA relaxation by Cas1-Cas2 occurred progressively, although not in a regular stepwise fashion.
source: DNA relaxation by Cas1-Cas2 occurred progressively, although not in a regular stepwise fashion (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from time course data in Figure 1D.

claim: The relaxation pattern was distinct from a topoisomerase I-generated ladder (ΔLk=+1), suggesting that the broken strand goes through multiple rotations before it is resealed.
source: The relaxation pattern was distinct from a topoisomerase I-generated ladder (ΔLk=+1) (Figure 1E), suggesting that the broken strand goes through multiple rotations before it is resealed.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data comparing Cas1-Cas2 relaxation to topoisomerase I activity.

claim: The topoisomer distribution of the Cas1-Cas2 plus protospacer treated supercoiled plasmid was more negatively supercoiled (ΔLk between −1 and −2) than that obtained from nick closure in the presence of dCas1-Cas2 and protospacer.
source: The topoisomer distribution of the Cas1-Cas2 plus protospacer treated supercoiled plasmid (Figure 1F; lane 8) was more negatively supercoiled (ΔLk between −1 and −2) than that obtained from nick closure in the presence of dCas1-Cas2 and protospacer (Figure 1F; lane 7) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from topological analysis in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The observed ΔLk between the Cas1-Cas2 relaxed and T4 ligase sealed plasmid distributions is consistent with the unwinding of a little more than one DNA turn within the target sequence during protospacer integration.
source: The observed ΔLk between the Cas1-Cas2 relaxed and T4 ligase sealed plasmid distributions (Figure 1F; Figure 1—figure supplement 2) is consistent with the unwinding of a little more than one DNA turn within the target sequence during protospacer integration.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the topological data from Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: L-R and R-S insertions were approximately equally prevalent in linear target sites, although L-R insertions were more abundant at very short time points.
source: L-R and R-S insertions were approximately equally prevalent, although L-R insertions were more abundant at very short time points.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from reactions with linear target sites.

claim: In vitro Cas1-Cas2 reactions showed no strand-specificity in protospacer integration.
source: Unlike orientation-specific protospacer integration in vivo, in vitro Cas1-Cas2 reactions showed no strand-specificity (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from reactions with linear target sites shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Csn2 or Cas9 or both failed to confer strand selectivity on Cas1-Cas2 reactions.
source: This bias-free insertion of the top or bottom strand from the protospacer was unchanged by the addition of Csn2 or Cas9 or both to the reactions (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from reactions with linear target sites shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: Csn2 and Cas9, singly or in combination, failed to stabilize protospacer integrations in the supercoiled plasmid target.
source: These proteins, singly or in combination, also failed to stabilize protospacer integrations in the supercoiled plasmid target (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from reactions with supercoiled plasmid targets shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The amount of the integration product was increased two- to threefold in the nicked target site compared to the normal product formed from the target without a nick.
source: The amount of the integration product (normal plus aberrant) was increased two- to threefold in comparison to the normal product formed from the target without a nick.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from reactions with nicked target sites.

claim: The native protospacer and the ones carrying T-insertions gave the predicted integration products at the L-R and R-S junctions with the native target site.
source: The native (T/T)0-protospacer as well as the ones carrying T-insertions, (T/T)n or (T/-)n, gave the predicted integration products at the L-R and R-S junctions with the native (T/T)0-target site (Figure 3B; lanes 2, 6, 10, and 14).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from reactions with modified protospacers and target sites shown in Figure 3B.

claim: For the modified target sites, integration occurred almost exclusively at the L-R junction.
source: For the (T/T)5, (T/T)10, and (T/T)15-targets, integration occurred almost exclusively at the L-R junction (Figure 3B; lanes 3–5, 7–9, 11–13, and 15–17).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from reactions with modified target sites shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Reactions of the modified protospacers with the modified target sites unveil a strict hierarchy in the choice of the L-R and R-S junctions during protospacer acquisition.
source: Reactions of the modified protospacers with the modified target sites unveil a strict hierarchy in the choice of the L-R and R-S junctions during protospacer acquisition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data with modified substrates.

claim: An R-S half-site was co-dominant with the 'minimal' L-R half-site when both were present in the same reaction.
source: Consistent with the independent recognition of the L-R and R-S junctions by the Cas1-Cas2 complex, an R-S half-site was co-dominant with the 'minimal' L-R half-site (containing 18 bp of the repeat; Figure 4—figure supplement 1) when both were present in the same reaction (Figure 4; lanes 15–18).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from reactions with half-target sites shown in Figure 4.

claim: The extension of the repeat segment in the minimal L-R half-site by 4 bp restored L-R dominance to the same degree as that displayed by the modified full linear targets.
source: However, the extension of the repeat segment in the minimal L-R half-site by 4 bp, L-R(+4) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), restored L-R dominance to the same degree as that displayed by the modified full linear targets (Figure 4; lanes 19–22).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from reactions with half-target sites shown in Figure 4.

claim: Cas1-Cas2 promoted the second integration step at the R-S junction in substrates mimicking semi-integration at the L-R junction, yielding the expected 81 nt product.
source: When the 5′-end of the unintegrated protospacer strand was labeled, integration was observed at the R-S junction (81 nt band) (Figure 5A; lanes 2–6).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from reactions with semi-integrated substrates shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Disintegration was more prominent than integration in semi-integrated substrates.
source: Strikingly, disintegration was more prominent than integration.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from reactions with semi-integrated substrates.

claim: Neither removing the leader strand nor placing a terminal 3′-dideoxy nucleotide eliminated or reduced the extent of integration at the R-S junction.
source: We attempted to block the disintegration competence of the leader strand in the substrate with the protospacer semi-integrated at the L-R junction by placing a terminal 3′-dideoxy nucleotide, or by removing this strand altogether. Neither of these substrate designs eliminated or reduced the extent of integration at the R-S junction (81 nt band in Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from reactions with modified semi-integrated substrates shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Disintegration occurred even in the absence of the leader strand.
source: However, labeling the 5′-end of the protospacer strand integrated at the L-R junction revealed that disintegration occurred even in the absence of the leader strand (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from reactions with modified semi-integrated substrates shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Water-mediated disintegration efficiency was ~40% of that of the 3′-hydroxyl and water combined.
source: Disintegration efficiency of water alone (in the absence of the leader strand) was ~40% of that of the 3′-hydroxyl and water combined (in the presence of the leader strand) (Figure 5C, compare lanes 2 and 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental finding from reactions with modified semi-integrated substrates shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Water is ~50% as competent a nucleophile as the 3′-hydroxyl for disintegration.
source: We note that water is ~50% as competent a nucleophile as the 3′-hydroxyl for disintegration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on water-mediated disintegration.

claim: Formation of the 5′-labeled 183 nt product (signifying no disintegration) was weak, though detectable, for the three trombone substrates tested.
source: Formation of the 5′-labeled 183 nt product (signifying no disintegration) was weak, though detectable, for the three substrates tested (Figure 6B; lanes 2, 4, and 6; Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from reactions with trombone substrates shown in Figure 6B.

claim: For all three trombone substrates labeled at the 3′-end, the shorter product (158 nt) exceeded the longer one (184 nt).
source: For all three substrates labeled at the 3′-end, the shorter product (158 nt) exceeded the longer one (184 nt) (Figure 6C; lanes 2, 4, and 6; Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from reactions with trombone substrates shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The maximum yield of the 158 nt product in the absence of a leader strand suggests that the second integration is more efficient when disintegration is performed by water rather than by the 3′-hydroxyl.
source: The maximum yield of the 158 nt product in the absence of a leader strand suggests that the second integration is more efficient when disintegration is performed by water rather than by the 3′-hydroxyl.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data from trombone substrate reactions.

claim: Integration of the second strand without disintegration of the first is quite infrequent.
source: First, integration of the second strand without disintegration of the first is quite infrequent.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the trombone substrate experiments.

claim: Disintegration of a protospacer from the L-R junction followed by its integration at the R-S junction in a two-step process is rare.
source: Second, disintegration of a protospacer from the L-R junction followed by its integration at the R-S junction in a two-step process is also rare.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the trombone substrate experiments.

claim: Integration of the second strand and disintegration of the first are most often concerted events.
source: Thus, integration of the second strand and disintegration of the first are most often concerted events, and two-ended insertion events by the Cas1-Cas2 complex seldom occur in vitro.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the trombone substrate experiments.

claim: Water being better at promoting disintegration coupled integration than the 3′-hydroxyl is significant.
source: Finally, water being better at promoting disintegration coupled integration than the 3′-hydroxyl is significant.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the trombone substrate experiments.

claim: The strand nick left unsealed during the water-mediated reaction would permit seemingly abortive intermediates to be processed by bacterial DNA repair systems into successful spacer insertion.
source: The strand nick left unsealed during the water-mediated reaction would permit seemingly abortive intermediates to be processed by bacterial DNA repair systems into successful spacer insertion (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation and speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Disintegration may be an important (but unappreciated) contributing factor in the adaption stage of CRISPR immunity.
source: Thus, paradoxically, disintegration may be an important (but unappreciated) contributing factor in the adaption stage of CRISPR immunity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The integration by Cas1-Cas2 in vitro starts with the insertion of one protospacer strand at the L-R junction, and utilizes a ruler-like mechanism to attempt integration of the second strand at the R-S junction.
source: Our analysis indicates that the integration by Cas1-Cas2 in vitro starts with the insertion of one protospacer strand at the L-R junction, and utilizes a ruler-like mechanism to attempt integration of the second strand at the R-S junction.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental findings.

claim: A successful second integration event is most often associated with the disintegration of the first one.
source: However, a successful second integration event is most often associated with the disintegration of the first one.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental findings.

claim: Two-ended protospacer integration, without intervening disintegration, is conceivable in vivo.
source: Two-ended protospacer integration, without intervening disintegration, is conceivable in vivo.
evidence: This is a speculation about the in vivo mechanism based on the in vitro findings.

claim: A high-order adaptation complex in which Cas1-Cas2 is assisted by additional Cas proteins and by bacterial factors may deter disintegration by coupling DNA processing to strand transfer without protospacer dissociation.
source: A high-order adaptation complex in which Cas1-Cas2 is assisted by additional Cas proteins (e.g., Cas4, Csn2, and Cascade/Cas9) and by bacterial factors (e.g., RecBCD and AddAb) (Amitai and Sorek, 2016; Nuñez et al., 2015a; Yosef et al., 2012; Heler et al., 2015; Wei et al., 2015a; Levy et al., 2015) may deter disintegration by coupling DNA processing to strand transfer without protospacer dissociation.
evidence: This is a speculation about the in vivo mechanism based on the in vitro findings and cited literature.

claim: Disintegration is generally viewed as antithetical to the completion of the two-strand transfer events during transposition reactions.
source: Disintegration is generally viewed as antithetical to the completion of the two-strand transfer events during transposition reactions, which are analogous to protospacer insertion at the CRISPR locus.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the Discussion.

claim: The in vitro Cas1-Cas2 reactions suggest that disintegration can generate DNA ends capable of triggering repair events that convert one-ended strand transfer intermediates into normal insertion products.
source: However, the in vitro Cas1-Cas2 reactions suggest that disintegration can generate DNA ends capable of triggering repair events that convert one-ended strand transfer intermediates into normal insertion products.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: A recent single-molecule FRET analysis suggests that the PSC formed during protospacer integration may be resolved by transcription from the CRISPR leader accompanied by limited DNA replication.
source: A recent single-molecule FRET analysis suggests that the PSC formed during protospacer integration may be resolved by transcription from the CRISPR leader accompanied by limited DNA replication (Budhathoki et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited evidence from another study.

claim: If the integration complex functions as a strand transfer-DNA repair machinery, the DNA ends may remain protected within it to be resolved rapidly.
source: However, if the integration complex functions as a strand transfer-DNA repair machinery, the DNA ends may remain protected within it to be resolved rapidly (Figure 7; pathway at the left).
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: An alternative solution to transcription/replication in simplifying PSC topology is the hydrolytic nicking of DNA (disintegration), allowing transposition (integration) to be completed by ensuing DNA repair.
source: The present study demonstrates that an alternative solution to transcription/replication in simplifying PSC topology is the hydrolytic nicking of DNA (disintegration), allowing transposition (integration) to be completed by ensuing DNA repair.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Disintegration may assist the movement of mini-transposons or short orphan transposons that are mobilized by ectopically supplied transposases.
source: In a general sense, disintegration may not be limited to spacer acquisition by CRISPR loci. It may assist the movement of mini-transposons or short orphan transposons that are mobilized by ectopically supplied transposases.
evidence: This is a speculation about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: Disintegration need not always be counterproductive even during normal transposition, provided the DNA repair machinery is able to recommence the interrupted reaction.
source: Disintegration need not always be counterproductive even during normal transposition, provided the DNA repair machinery is able to recommence the interrupted reaction.
evidence: This is a speculation about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: The Cas1-Cas2 system highlights the resourcefulness of biological catalysis in repurposing an apparently abortive reaction toward a physiologically meaningful outcome.
source: The Cas1-Cas2 system highlights the resourcefulness of biological catalysis in repurposing an apparently abortive reaction toward a physiologically meaningful outcome.
evidence: This is a concluding statement summarizing the significance of the findings.
